content: Numerous medications are available for the acute treatment of migraines in adults, and some of these have been approved for use in children and adolescents in outpatient settings. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of pharmacological treatments for migraines in individuals aged 17 years or younger. For this review, children were defined as those under 12 years of age, while adolescents were defined as those aged 12 to 17 years. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared medications for acute migraine relief with placebo in children and adolescents. A total of 27 RCTs were identified, involving 9158 participants, of whom 7630 received medication. The mean age of participants ranged from 8.2 to 14.7 years. Most studies focused on triptan-class drugs, including almotriptan, eletriptan, naratriptan, rizatriptan, sumatriptan, sumatriptan combined with naproxen sodium, and zolmitriptan. Other medications studied included ibuprofen, paracetamol (acetaminophen), and dihydroergotamine (DHE). Adverse event data were reported in all but one study. The quality of evidence, assessed using the GRADE criteria, was generally low to moderate, primarily due to imprecision and inconsistency. Ibuprofen was found to be more effective than placebo in achieving pain freedom at two hours in two small studies involving 162 children (risk ratio [RR] 1.87, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.15 to 3.04). However, the evidence was of low quality due to imprecision. Paracetamol, on the other hand, was not found to be superior to placebo in one small study involving 80 children. Triptans as a class were shown to be more effective than placebo in achieving pain freedom. In three studies involving 273 children, triptans demonstrated a risk ratio of 1.67 (95% CI 1.06 to 2.62) with a number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) of 13. In 21 studies involving 7026 adolescents, triptans had a risk ratio of 1.32 (95% CI 1.19 to 1.47) with an NNTB of 6. The quality of evidence for these findings was moderate. There was no significant difference in the effectiveness of triptans between children and adolescents. Triptans were associated with an increased risk of minor, non-serious adverse events in adolescents (risk difference [RD] 0.13, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.18, number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome [NNTH] 8). However, no serious adverse events were reported. In children, the risk of minor adverse events was not statistically significant (RD 0.06, 95% CI −0.04 to 0.17, NNTH 17). Sumatriptan combined with naproxen sodium was found to be superior to placebo in one study involving 490 adolescents (RR 3.25, 95% CI 1.78 to 5.94, NNTB 6). The evidence for this finding was of moderate quality. Oral dihydroergotamine was not found to be superior to placebo in one small study involving 13 children. In conclusion, low-quality evidence from two small trials suggests that ibuprofen may improve pain freedom in children with migraines. However, there is limited information on the adverse events associated with ibuprofen in these trials. Triptans as a class are effective in providing pain relief in both children and adolescents but are associated with higher rates of minor adverse events. Sumatriptan combined with naproxen sodium is also effective in treating migraines in adolescents.
